cards.back:
Suppose there is some unknown probability distribution $\mu$ on pairs $(x,y) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$. We observe a finite dataset $$\mathcal{D}=\{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_N,y_N)\},$$ whose examples are sampled independently from $\mu$. The aim is to use $\mathcal{D}$ to find a function $h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ that performs well on new examples drawn from the same distribution.

If the output is completely determined by some unknown function $f$, then $y=f(x)$. The joint-distribution framework also allows for noise or uncertainty in the output.

cards.front: What is the typical approach to the general learning problem?
cards.back:
The typical approach is as follows:

1. Select some “parameter space” $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$ for some $p \in \mathbb{N}$.

2. Choose some function $H: \mathcal{X} \times \Theta \to \mathcal{Y}$, which we will call a “model”.

3. Choose some function $J: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$, which we will call a “loss function”. This function should, in some reasonable way, indicate how close two elements of $\mathcal{Y}$ are to one another. We have purposely not used the word metric here, as this loss function does not need to satisfy all the properties of a metric.

4. Based on the dataset $\mathcal{D}$, choose some $\theta \in \Theta$ so that $h_\theta(x) = H(x, \theta)$ predicts $y$ well in terms of the loss function $J$. That is, we want to minimize something that looks like $$\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x, y) \in \mathcal{D}} J(y, h_\theta(x)).$$

cards.front: What is the expected loss of a model?
cards.back: Suppose that $(x,y)$ is a new example sampled from the unknown distribution $\mu$. The loss $J(y,h_\theta(x))$ tells us how well the model performs on this particular example. Its average performance over all possible examples is measured by the expected loss $$R(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\left[J(y,h_\theta(x))\right].$$ This is also called the true risk or population risk. Ideally, we would like to choose $\theta$ to make this quantity as small as possible.

cards.front: What is the empirical loss of a model?
cards.back: The distribution $\mu$ is unknown, so we cannot usually calculate the expected loss directly. Instead, we average the loss over the examples in the dataset $\mathcal{D}$: $$\widehat{R}_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}J(y,h_\theta(x)).$$ This is called the empirical loss or empirical risk. Unlike the expected loss, it can be calculated from the data we have observed.

cards.front: Why might minimizing empirical loss produce a good model?
cards.back:
Because the examples in $\mathcal{D}$ are sampled from $\mu$, we hope that the empirical loss is a good approximation of the expected loss. If this is true, then a model with small empirical loss should also perform well on new examples.

This is not automatic: a model may fit the observed data very well while performing poorly on new data. A central aim of learning theory is to understand when, and by how much, empirical loss can be expected to approximate expected loss.
